title: The Merge That Quietly Invented $125 of Revenue
partialText:
Inside the Python Data Stack — Part 6

Why pandas can give you perfectly valid DataFrames with completely wrong answers

Here’s a bug with actual financial consequences, and it produces zero errors, zero warnings, and a DataFrame that looks completely normal.

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    'order_id': [101, 102, 103, 104],
    'customer_id': [1, 2, 1, 3],
    'amount': [50.0, 20.0, 75.0, 10.0],
})

# a customer table that's supposed to have one row per customer --
# except customer 1 has two rows, from some upstream data issue
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    'customer_id': [1, 1, 2, 3],
    'email': ['a@x.com', 'a@x.com', 'b@x.com', 'c@x.com'],
    'signup_channel': ['web', 'referral', 'web', 'app'],
})
merged = orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left')

orders has 4 rows. merged has 6.

print(orders['amount'].sum())    # 155.0  -- correct
print(merged['amount'].sum())    # 280.0  -- wrong

Nothing crashed. The merge did exactly what a left join on customer_id is defined to do: for every match on the right side, produce a row. Customer 1 matched twice, so order 101's $50 and order 103's $75 each got duplicated. If this merged table then feeds into any kind of groupby(...).sum() for a revenue report, that report is now overstating revenue by $125, and there is nothing in the pipeline that will tell you.

(Environment for this post: Python 3.12.3, pandas 3.0.2, NumPy 2.4.4, same sandbox as Part 5. Methodology: every timing is the minimum of several repeated calls using time.perf_counter, not a single run and not timeit/%timeit — the reasoning for why is its own section in Part 4. Row counts, group counts, and window sizes are stated at each benchmark below, ratios are the point, absolute milliseconds will move around on different hardware.)

The fix nobody uses until they’ve been burned once

Pandas has a parameter specifically for this, and I didn’t reliably use it myself until after a version of this exact bug cost someone an afternoon of “why don’t these numbers reconcile”:

orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left', validate='many_to_one')
MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge
Duplicates in right:
  customer_id
           1 ...

validate checks your assumption about the relationship — 'one_to_one', 'one_to_many', 'many_to_one', or 'many_to_many' — against what the data actually looks like, and refuses to proceed if they don't match. It costs you nothing at merge time and it turns a silent, downstream, dollar-figure bug into an immediate, loud, traceback-at-the-source bug. I now put validate= on essentially every merge where I have an assumption about cardinality, which in practice is almost all of them — "this should be one row per customer" is a claim, and claims are exactly the kind of thing worth checking rather than trusting.

That merge bug was really a shape bug wearing a data-correctness costume — the row count changed silently, and everything downstream inherited the wrong shape without complaint. That turns out to be the thread connecting everything else in this post: apply() further down can silently change the shape of what comes back from a groupby. MultiIndex is what happens when pandas needs to encode more than one dimension into a single index. And unstack(), at the very end, is what happens when you change that shape back without touching the values underneath it at all. Shape, not just values, is something worth tracking deliberately in pandas — it's rarely enforced for you the way a schema might be.

MultiIndex is the same trick as category, one level up

Group by two columns and look at what comes back:

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'region': ['east', 'east', 'west', 'west', 'east'],
    'product': ['a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a'],
    'sales': [10, 20, 30, 40, 15],
})
grouped = df.groupby(['region', 'product'])['sales'].sum()
print(type(grouped.index))
print(grouped.index.levels)
print(grouped.index.codes)
<class 'pandas.MultiIndex'>
[['east', 'west'], ['a', 'b']]
[[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0, 1]]

Here’s that structure laid out end to end — the result you see versus the levels-and-codes it’s actually built from, and why that structure lets reshaping avoid repeating work a naive approach would redo:

This is exactly the category structure from Part 5 — a small table of unique values (levels), plus a compact array of integer codes pointing into it — just applied to an index instead of a column. Once this clicks, a fact from later in this post stops being a surprise: reshaping a MultiIndexed result (unstack, stack) can be substantially cheaper than it looks, because pandas already has the unique values and the codes describing how they combine, and can lay that existing structure out differently instead of re-deriving it from raw rows. It's not a zero-copy trick the way NumPy's reshape from Part 1 is — the values still get moved into a new layout — but it operates on the already-aggregated representation rather than starting over, which is the part that matters for speed.

apply() and transform() are not interchangeable, even when they look like they should be

Shape again, this time inside a single groupby call rather than across a merge — and this one’s a correctness trap before it’s a performance one. Group-wise z-score, two ways:

r_apply = df.groupby('group')['value'].apply(lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std())
r_transform = df.groupby('group')['value'].transform(lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std())

Same math, same lambda, wildly different shape coming back:

r_apply.index:
MultiIndex([(1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4), (2, 5)],
           names=['group', None])

r_transform.index:
RangeIndex(start=0, stop=6, step=1)

apply(), when the function returns something the same length as each group, stitches the results back together with the group label added as an extra index level. transform() is specifically built to return something aligned to the originalDataFrame's index, ready to assign straight back as a column. Try df['zscore'] = df.groupby('group')['value'].apply(...) and you're assigning a MultiIndexed Series into a flat-indexed column — it'll either misalign or fail outright, depending on what else is going on, and either way it's not what you wanted.

The cleaner way to state the actual rule, rather than “apply is per-group, transform is per-row”: transform() guarantees its output is aligned to the original index, one way or another — hand it a function that returns a single scalar per group, and it broadcasts that scalar back out to every row in the group automatically. apply() makes no such guarantee; it's more general, and the shape you get back depends entirely on what your function returns. Give apply() a scalar-returning function and you get one row per group with a plain index, no MultiIndex involved at all — the awkward extra index level specifically shows up when your function returns something the same length as the group, because that's the one case where apply() has to decide how to stitch per-row results back together, and it does so by keeping the group label around. If you want a guaranteed shape without having to think about which case you're in, transform() is the one built for that; apply() is for when you genuinely want the flexibility and are prepared to check what shape came back.

Once you’re using the right tool for the shape you want, performance has its own twist. On 200,000 rows across 500 groups:

groupby.apply(lambda):            113.26 ms
groupby.transform(lambda):        123.34 ms
groupby.transform('mean'/'std'):    5.47 ms

transform() with a lambda isn't faster than apply() with one — if anything it was slightly slower here, and I checked this wasn't a fluke by rerunning it several times. Both are still calling a Python function once per group. The 20x win only shows up when you drop the lambda entirely and hand pandas the string name of a built-in aggregation ('mean', 'std'), which lets it use its own optimized per-group implementation instead of calling back into Python at all. This is the exact np.vectorize lesson from Part 2, transplanted into pandas: the name of the method you reach for (apply vs transform) controls correctness and shape; whether you actually get the speed depends on whether you handed it a real vectorized path or just a Python function wearing a pandas method as a costume.

rolling().apply() has a parameter that's worth more than the method itself

Window functions are where this lesson shows up most dramatically. Rolling mean over 200,000 points, window size 20:

rolling.mean() builtin:               3.07 ms
rolling.apply(mean, raw=True):       576.32 ms
rolling.apply(mean, raw=False):     4896.41 ms

The built-in .rolling(20).mean() is a compiled loop — implemented in Cython, the same category as the ufuncs from Part 2 — with no per-window Python function calls at all. .rolling(20).apply(...) calls your Python function once per window regardless, which is already 188x slower even in its best configuration. That "best configuration" is raw=True, which hands your function a plain NumPy array for each window. Leave it at the default, raw=False, and pandas wraps every single window in a full Series — with its own index — before calling your function, the same per-row Series construction tax from iterrows() in Part 5, just paid once per window instead of once per row. That default costs you another 8.5x on top of the 188x you already lost by not using the built-in. If you ever have to use rolling().apply() with your own function, raw=Truecosts you nothing and avoids most of that overhead the instant your function doesn't actually need the index or Seriesmethods — which, if you're doing numeric window math, it almost never does.

Reshaping: unstack versus redoing the work

Last one, and it ties directly back to the MultiIndex section above. If you already have a grouped, MultiIndexed result, reshaping it should be substantially cheaper than redoing the aggregation:

grouped = df.groupby(['region', 'product'])['sales'].sum()
grouped.unstack('product')                                          # 0.281 ms
df.pivot_table(index='region', columns='product', values='sales', aggfunc='sum')  # 36.825 ms

Same output, verified equal, on 200,000 rows grouped into 4 regions × 3 products — 131x apart. unstack() operates on the levels-and-codes structure that's already sitting there, laying it out differently without re-deriving it. pivot_table() doesn't know you already did the aggregation — it re-runs the full groupby from the raw rows every time you call it. If you find yourself calling pivot_table on data you've already grouped, that's a sign to reach for unstack instead; if you're starting from raw rows and haven't grouped yet, pivot_table is doing necessary work, not wasted work — the trap is specifically re-deriving something you already have.

Where this goes next

Every technique in this post assumes you already know roughly what shape and scale your data is in. Part 7 is where that stops being assumed and starts being engineered on purpose — turning raw columns into the kind of features a model can actually use, at a point in the pipeline where the memory and dtype habits from Part 5, and the join and reshape habits from this post, all have to hold up under real data volume at once.

title: AWS Bedrock Getting Started — Serverless Inference and Cross-Region Invocation in Practice
partialText:
Background

In my previous articles, I shared a lot about AI services on Azure Foundry. From here on, I plan to expand into AWS as well. In this article, I will share what I learned from my first hands-on session with AWS Bedrock: the differences between Azure Foundry and AWS Bedrock, with more focus on Bedrock itself. The content today is fairly basic, but as the saying goes, every great building starts from the ground up — every achievement begins with a small first step!

After reading this post, you should understand how Bedrock’s serverless model inference works, what inference profiles are for, and how to call models with the AWS SDK.

AWS Bedrock

Bedrock is AWS's AI service platform. Its positioning is similar to Azure Foundry: foundation models, agent development and deployment, RAG knowledge bases, GenAI safety and risk services, model fine-tuning, evaluation, and more. In this article, let's start with the foundation model service.

Access Bedrock

Before we get into the technical details, there is one prerequisite worth mentioning: as an individual developer, you cannot access the Bedrock platform by default. You need to submit company business registration information to AWS.

Only after approval can you get access.

That does add some friction for individual developers!

Alright — let’s move into the technical discussion.

Serverless Model Inference

If you have read my previous articles about Azure Foundry, you already know that Foundry manages large models through projects. If your agent needs an online model for inference, you first create a Foundry Project, then create a Deployment for the specific model you want to use.

For foundation models, Bedrock takes a different approach: Serverless. In other words, you do not need to deploy anything before you can use model resources directly.

Of course, Bedrock also supports flexible custom deployment options for these scenarios:

  • Provisioned Throughput: compared with Serverless mode, Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model capacity for you. It is billed hourly rather than per token, which makes it a good fit for stable, high-traffic, latency-sensitive workloads.
  • Fine-tuned models: models you train on your domain data within the Bedrock platform.
  • Imported models: model weights trained on another platform — for example, on AWS SageMaker — and then imported into Bedrock.

For today, we will stick with Serverless mode: just specify a model ID in code. On Bedrock, model IDs come in two formats:

  • Base Model ID: this is straightforward — it identifies the vendor's model and generally follows the format {provider}.{model-name}-{version}:{iteration}, for example amazon.nova-pro-v1:0.
  • Inference Profile ID: on top of the base format, a geography prefix such as us, eu, or apac is added, producing IDs like us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0. Let's look at what that is for in the next section.

Model Inference Profiles

Inference Profiles are another AWS resource type. Bedrock provides predefined profiles called Cross-Region Inference, such as us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0.

When you use this kind of Cross-Region Inference profile as your model ID, Bedrock automatically routes requests across different regions within the same geography based on load and availability.

For example, under the us geography, routing can happen across regions such as us-east-1, us-east-2, and us-west-2. That gives you higher throughput and better availability. Smart design, right?

In our example, we define two models:

MODELS = {
    "Amazon Nova Pro": "us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0",
    "Amazon Nova 2 Lite": "us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0",
}
DEFAULT_MODEL = "Amazon Nova Pro"

Great — with these concepts in place, we can move on to the code demo.

Creating a Bedrock Client with the AWS SDK

For Bedrock development, there is no separate SDK. You use AWS's unified SDK package boto3, then create a Bedrock client from it, like this:

import boto3  # AWS SDK for Python
session = boto3.Session()
region = session.region_name
bedrock = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=region)

AWS Authentication

The boto3.Session() call above tries to resolve your credential information for authentication. During development, we can authenticate with the AWS CLI. It stores credentials locally, and boto3 can pick them up afterward.

aws login

Source Region vs Destination Region

In this article, we use cross-region inference profiles to specify models, which introduces two concepts: source region and destination region.

The source region is the region your client connects to first. In our example, that comes from the session — decided when you log in. I chose us-east-1:

region = session.region_name

The destination region is where Bedrock actually routes the request — for example, us-east-2.

Here is a trap worth watching out for: the region you authenticate against must fall within the geography of the cross-region inference profile you choose, or the call will fail. If my region is us-east-1, I can only use the us geography prefix — not eu!

Invoke API vs Converse API

The Bedrock client gives you two APIs for calling large models:

  • Invoke API: a lower-level interface that talks directly to each vendor's model. Because different models have different requirements, you need to prepare prompts and parameters accordingly.
  • Converse API: a higher-level interface with a unified request format. Bedrock handles model-specific adaptation underneath, so it is more developer-friendly.

Here is how Invoke API looks:

text_to_summarize = "many text here omit..."
prompt = f"""Please provide a summary of the following text. Do not add any information that is not mentioned in the text below.
<text>
{text_to_summarize}
</text>
"""
nova_body = json.dumps(
    {
        "schemaVersion": "messages-v1",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": prompt}]}],
        "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 1000, "temperature": 0.5},
    }
)
response = bedrock.invoke_model(
    modelId=MODELS[DEFAULT_MODEL],
    body=nova_body,
    accept="application/json",
    contentType="application/json",
)
response_body = json.loads(response.get("body").read())
# Extract and display the response text
nova_summary = response_body["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]

And here is the Converse API version:

converse_request = {
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "text": f"Please provide a concise summary of the following text in 2-3 sentences. Text to summarize: {text_to_summarize}"
                }
            ],
        }
    ],
    "inferenceConfig": {
        "maxTokens": 500,
        "temperature": 0.4,
    },
}

response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId=MODELS[DEFAULT_MODEL],
    messages=converse_request["messages"],
    inferenceConfig=converse_request["inferenceConfig"],
)
# Extract the model's response
model_converse_response = response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]

Summary

In this article, we covered the basics of getting started with AWS Bedrock:

  • Bedrock’s access requirements for individual developers
  • How Serverless inference differs from Azure Foundry's project-and-deployment model
  • The difference between Base Model ID and Inference Profile ID
  • How Cross-Region Inference improves throughput and availability
  • Setting up boto3, authenticating with the AWS CLI, and understanding source vs destination regions
  • Choosing between the lower-level Invoke API and the unified Converse API

In upcoming articles, I will continue exploring more AWS AI services and share what I learn along the way.

I’m Chris Bao, a software engineer focused on Azure and AWS AI platforms, specializing in AI services and agent development on both clouds.

I offer training and consulting for organizations and individuals. For collaboration, please contact: baoqger@gmail.com

title: The Base M4 Mac Mini Is a Better Local AI Machine Than Most People Realize
partialText:
It will not replace a large cloud model or a workstation with a huge GPU. It does make a surprisingly good private machine for the work that happens every day

The conversation around local AI often becomes silly in two opposite directions. One group talks as if a small desktop Mac can replace every paid AI service. The other dismisses local models because they cannot run the largest reasoning model, render a long video, and index a company archive at the same time.

Both miss the more useful question: what work would I rather keep on my own machine?

For a lot of people, that answer is not a science-fiction agent rebuilding an entire codebase overnight. It is a private chat window for rough ideas. It is an assistant that can summarize a meeting transcript without sending it to another vendor. It is OCR for a stack of scans, a model that can read a screenshot, speech-to-text for interviews, or a small coding helper when Wi-Fi is unreliable. These are ordinary jobs, which is exactly why they matter.

The base M4 Mac mini has a real ceiling. Its unified memory is shared by macOS, your apps, and the model. You cannot ignore that ceiling by saying “Apple Silicon” enough times. But the machine is fast, quiet, small, and already sitting on many desks. Used with sensible expectations, it is one of the least painful ways to begin running useful AI locally.

The important limit is memory, not ambition

People coming from cloud AI are used to treating a model choice like a dropdown menu. Choose the biggest option, wait a little longer, and somebody else’s infrastructure absorbs the cost. Local AI is more physical. The model has to live in memory. Its context has to live in memory. The operating system still needs room to breathe. If you are also running a browser with forty tabs, an IDE, Docker, and a video call, the machine does not suddenly become more capable because you want it to be.

That is why a base Mac mini works best when it is treated as a focused appliance rather than an all-you-can-eat AI buffet. Run one substantial task at a time. Close the model when you move from document work to image generation. Keep an eye on the context window instead of assuming a huge advertised number will be comfortable on a modest-memory machine.

This is not a defect unique to Apple hardware. It is simply the part that cloud products hide. A local workflow forces you to think about capacity, which can be a healthy habit. The model that fits comfortably and responds quickly is usually more useful than the theoretically smarter one that turns every question into a wait.

Small models have become good enough for the boring work

There is a strange bias in AI discussions toward dramatic tasks. We judge a model by whether it can solve a difficult programming puzzle, write a flawless research paper, or beat another model on a benchmark. Those comparisons are interesting, but a lot of daily value comes from much less glamorous work.

A well-chosen small language model can turn a rough meeting note into actions and owners. It can help reorganize a draft, explain a terminal command, compare two versions of a policy, or produce a first pass at a short script. A coding model in the same size range can be useful for a function, a test, an unfamiliar regular expression, or a quick explanation of code that has been in the repository for years.

The key is to give these models bounded jobs. I would not ask one to autonomously redesign a production service. I would ask it to work beside me on a specific patch, then I would read the output and run the test suite. That is a much more realistic relationship with local AI. It is not a replacement for judgment. It is a fast assistant that costs nothing after the machine is on your desk and does not need a network connection to be helpful.

Privacy becomes practical when the workflow stays local

“Private” gets used too casually in AI marketing. A service can have a respectable policy and still require you to upload a document, create an account, accept a retention setting, and trust a chain of infrastructure that you cannot see. For many tasks that trade-off is reasonable. I use cloud tools too. But some work feels different once it includes client notes, internal planning, personal journals, interview audio, financial files, or an unfinished idea I am not ready to put on a server.

Local models offer a more concrete promise: if the workflow is properly configured, the data can stay on the Mac. That does not remove the need for normal security. A laptop can be lost, backups can be exposed, and a poorly chosen application may still have network features turned on. It does, however, give you a meaningful boundary. You can work on sensitive material without converting every question into an upload.

This is where local retrieval can be genuinely useful. Give a local tool a folder of documents, let it build an index, then ask narrow questions against that collection. The results will not always be as polished as a large cloud system. They also need checking, especially when the answer joins information from multiple documents. But for finding the right paragraph, locating a name, or pulling an answer with a citation back to a file, it can be a far better experience than hunting through Finder.

The best local stack is usually a chain, not one giant model

The most compelling local setup is not a single chatbot trying to do every job. It is a few modest tools connected in a useful order.

An audio model turns a meeting into text. A language model extracts decisions and open questions. A text-to-speech tool reads the summary while you walk. A vision model turns a photographed receipt or whiteboard into searchable text. An embedding model makes the result retrievable later. None of these components has to be enormous. The value comes from passing the right output to the next step without spraying the raw material across five different accounts.

This is also a better way to judge local AI. Instead of asking whether one model beats a cloud assistant in every category, ask whether it removes a small piece of friction from a recurring workflow. Saving ten minutes on every interview or avoiding a manual transcription service can matter more than winning an abstract model comparison.

The engineering work is in the hand-off. Make sure the transcription has a sensible file name. Keep the original audio. Check the summary against the source before acting on it. Give the model a small enough input that it does not lose the plot. Local tools become dependable when the workflow around them is clear.

Image and video are where the trade-offs become visible

Text, speech, OCR, and document tasks are usually the comfortable territory for a base Mac mini. Image generation can also be enjoyable if you choose a model and resolution that fit the machine, accept a longer render, and avoid opening every other heavy application at the same time. This is a pleasant bonus for concept images, personal projects, thumbnails, and experiments. It is not an excuse to pretend every local image model will feel as quick as a large cloud service.

Video is the line where I would stop making promises. Modern generative video models are hungry for memory and time, especially when the job includes high resolution, many frames, or sound. You may be able to experiment, but it is not the workload I would recommend as the reason to buy the smallest configuration. If local video is central to your work, more unified memory changes the conversation more than any clever installation guide.

That distinction is worth keeping. A machine can be excellent for local AI without being excellent for every form of AI. The honest version is more useful because it helps people buy and build for the work they will actually do.

The setup should be boring before it becomes clever

The easiest way to make local AI frustrating is to install six apps, download ten models, and begin comparing token counts before you have completed one useful task. I would start with a single local runner that makes model downloads and conversations simple. Then pick one text model that fits comfortably, one task you care about, and a small test you can repeat.

For example, take a real meeting recording that you are allowed to process. Transcribe it locally. Ask the language model for action items. Check the names and dates yourself. Save the transcript next to the original file. If that works, you have a workflow, not just a demo. The next addition might be document search, a coding assistant, or an OCR tool. Add it because you found a recurring use, not because a benchmark chart made it look impressive.

I also prefer tools that make it easy to remove a model and start again. Local AI is changing quickly. The model that feels perfect this month may be overtaken soon, and a locked-in setup is just another kind of cloud dependency. Keep the data folders understandable, document the commands you rely on, and avoid turning experimentation into a fragile pile of scripts.

A smaller private machine changes the question

The base M4 Mac mini will not end the need for cloud AI. Large models remain better at difficult reasoning, broad synthesis, and work that benefits from enormous context or serious compute. The point is not to deny that advantage. The point is to stop sending every modest task there by default.

There is a category of AI work that benefits from being immediate, cheap to repeat, and close to the files it needs. A small local model can occupy that category well. It can help before a draft leaves your desk. It can process an audio file on a flight. It can search personal notes without turning them into product telemetry. It can be slow in a way that is still acceptable because nobody is charging by the token or waiting for an account to load.

That is the real appeal of the little Mac mini. It is not a secret supercomputer. It is a practical computer that can now keep more of your AI work in your own hands. For plenty of people, that is the upgrade worth noticing.
